title: An organiser that matches the text
statement: Give learners a graphic organiser matched to the text's structure, such as a Venn diagram for comparison or a timeline for sequence, and reuse it for their speaking and writing.
example: One design maps 4 structures to organisers: comparison to a Venn diagram, cause to a chain, sequence to a timeline and narrative to a story map.
detail: A reading course's review standard, citing IES videos on reading skills in grades 5 to 8 and on early reading outcomes for English learners, makes structure-matched organisers available as comprehension scaffolds (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/g3-reading-red-team/references/teaching-moves/graphic-organizers-and-no-ability-label.md`). An organiser makes the text's relationships visible, so learners see them as well as read them, and the filled organiser becomes the source for speaking and writing. A mismatched organiser, such as a Venn diagram on a sequential text, misleads, so the standard checks that the organiser's type matches the passage's structure.

evidence.quote: a graphic organizer is gonna help make those relationships clearer because they're not only going to read it in the graphic organizer, they're gonna see it in the graphic organizer. And that will make the content more comprehensible. And it also serves as a source for writing and speaking activities.
Structure-matched graphic organizers (sequence, compare/contrast, cause-effect, Venn, story map) are available as comprehension scaffolds
(a Venn diagram slapped on a sequential text) actively misleads
compare→Venn, cause→cause-effect chain, sequence→timeline/steps, narrative→story map
